lessons.title: Sound as a wave
lessons.summary: Amplitude, frequency, period, wavelength and phase; the sine wave formula; and the two numbers every oscillator needs, samples per period and phase increment.
lessons.body:
Every sound your synth makes ends up as a speaker cone pushing air back and forth. The air pressure at your ear rises and falls around normal atmospheric pressure, and your ear turns that pattern into what you hear.

Inside the synth there is no air. There is first a sequence of numbers, then a voltage on a wire. The vocabulary is the same at every stage, though. A *wave* is a quantity (pressure, voltage, or a number in memory) that changes over time, and we describe it by how big the change is, how often it repeats and where in its cycle it is.

This lesson sets up that vocabulary and the one formula you'll use constantly: the sine wave.

## The four basic measurements

Picture one repeating cycle of a wave plotted against time:

```diagram
 +A |    .-'''-.
    |  .'       '.
  0 +-'-----------'.-----------.-> t
    |               '.       .'
 -A |                 '-...-'
    |<------- one period T ----->|
```

- **Amplitude (A)** is how far the wave swings from its centre line. In air that's a pressure difference; in a circuit it's volts; in software it's a number, conventionally between −1 and +1. Bigger amplitude sounds louder, though loudness perception is more complicated than amplitude alone.
- **Period (T)** is the time one full cycle takes, in seconds.
- **Frequency (f)** is how many cycles happen per second, in hertz (Hz). It's the reciprocal of the period (one divided by the period).
- **Wavelength (λ)** is the *distance* one cycle covers as it travels through a medium such as air.

Frequency and period are two views of the same thing: if you know how long one cycle takes, you know how many fit in a second.

```formula
f = 1 / T
f = 1 / 0.00227 s
f ≈ 440 Hz
where
f: the frequency, in hertz (Hz): how many complete cycles happen each second
T: the period, the time one complete cycle takes, in seconds (s); here about 0.00227 s (2.27 ms)
s: seconds
Hz: hertz, the unit of frequency: one cycle per second
≈: approximately equal to (the numbers are rounded)
In words: frequency is one divided by the period, so a shorter cycle means a higher frequency. Halve the period and the frequency doubles.
```

Turned round, the period is one divided by the frequency: a 440 Hz wave has a period of 1/440 s, about 2.27 milliseconds (ms). The relationship is exact for any repeating wave; it only stops being meaningful for sounds that don't repeat, such as noise.

Wavelength needs one more ingredient, the speed at which the wave travels. In the time of one period, the wave moves forward by one wavelength:

```formula
λ = c / f
λ = 343 / 440
λ ≈ 0.78 m
where
λ: lambda, the wavelength: the distance one cycle occupies as it travels, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound in the medium, in metres per second (m/s); about 343 m/s in dry air at 20 °C
f: the frequency of the wave, in hertz (Hz)
m: metres
m/s: metres per second
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the wavelength is the speed of sound divided by the frequency, so higher notes have shorter wavelengths. A 440 Hz tone in air has a wavelength of about 0.78 m.
```

The speed of sound depends on the medium and its temperature (it is faster in warmer air and much faster in water or steel), so λ is only defined for sound actually travelling through something.

Wavelength matters for room acoustics and speaker design (why bass travels through walls, why rooms have resonances). Inside a synth it barely matters at all: your signals live as samples and voltages, where only time and frequency count. Don't confuse *wavelength* with *period*. One is metres, the other seconds.

Human hearing is usually quoted as roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz (20,000 Hz). The top end falls with age, and that range is a rule of thumb rather than a hard limit. In air, those frequencies have wavelengths of roughly 17 m down to 1.7 cm.

## Phase and radians

The **phase of a wave** says *where in its cycle* it is at a given moment. You can measure it in fractions of a cycle (0 to 1), degrees (0° to 360°), or **radians** (0 to 2π). Maths libraries use radians, so get comfortable with them.

A radian comes from the unit circle (a circle of radius 1). Walk around it: a full lap is a distance of 2π, so one cycle is 2π radians. Converting is a single multiplication:

```formula
θ = 2 × π × p
θ = 2 × π × 0.25
θ ≈ 1.571 rad
where
θ: theta, the phase as an angle, in radians (rad)
p: the phase as a fraction of a cycle, from 0 up to 1; here a quarter of a cycle, 0.25
π: pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159
rad: radians, the angle unit maths libraries use; 2π rad is one full cycle, the same as 360°
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: to turn a fraction of a cycle into radians, multiply by 2π. A quarter of a cycle is π/2, about 1.571 radians, which is 90°.
```

| Cycles | Degrees | Radians |
|---|---|---|
| 0.25 | 90° | π/2 ≈ 1.571 |
| 0.5 | 180° | π ≈ 3.142 |
| 1 | 360° | 2π ≈ 6.283 |

Phase matters most when you **combine** waves. Two identical sines in phase add up to double the amplitude. Shift one by half a cycle (π radians, 180°) and they cancel completely. Anywhere in between gives partial reinforcement or partial cancellation. That's why detuned oscillators "beat", and why some layered sounds go thin when a phase relationship shifts.

Phase on its own, for a single steady tone, is mostly inaudible. Your ear can't tell a sine from the same sine starting a quarter-cycle later. What you *can* hear is a sudden phase **jump** in the middle of a tone: the waveform jumps to a new value instantly, and you hear a click.

## The sine wave formula

The purest tone is a sine wave. This formula gives its value at any moment, and it is the starting point for every oscillator in the project:

```formula
x(t) = A × sin(2 × π × f × t + φ)
where
x(t): the value of the wave at time t: a pressure, a voltage or a sample value, depending on where the wave lives
t: the time since the wave started, in seconds (s)
A: the amplitude, the largest value the wave reaches; in software usually at most 1.0
sin: the sine function, which turns an angle in radians into a value that swings smoothly between −1 and +1 and repeats every 2π
π: pi, about 3.14159
f: the frequency, in hertz (Hz), cycles per second
φ: phi, the starting phase, in radians (rad): where in the cycle the wave is at t = 0
In words: count how many cycles have passed (f × t), turn that into an angle (× 2π), add the starting phase, take the sine, and scale it by the amplitude.
```

Read it from the inside out:

1. **f·t** is the number of cycles completed after t seconds. At 440 Hz, after 0.01 s you've done 4.4 cycles.
2. **2π·f·t** converts cycles to radians, because `sin` wants radians.
3. **φ** (phi) is the starting phase, in radians. A starting phase of π/2 turns a sine into a cosine.
4. **A** scales the result, which otherwise swings between −1 and +1.

For example, take an amplitude of 0.5, a frequency of 440 Hz and a starting phase of 0, and ask for the value half a millisecond in:

```formula
x(t) = A × sin(2 × π × f × t + φ)
x = 0.5 × sin(2 × π × 440 × 0.0005 + 0)
x = 0.5 × sin(1.382)
x ≈ 0.491
where
x(t): the value of the wave at time t
x: the same value, written without the (t) once t is fixed
A: the amplitude; here 0.5
sin: the sine function, taking radians
π: pi, about 3.14159
f: the frequency; here 440 Hz
t: the time; here 0.0005 s (half a millisecond), by which point 0.22 cycles have passed
φ: phi, the starting phase; here 0 radians
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 0.22 of a cycle is an angle of about 1.382 radians, whose sine is about 0.982, and half of that is about 0.491.
```

The formula describes an ideal, never-ending tone; real notes start, stop and change, which is what the rest of the module deals with.

The term **2πf** comes up so often that it has its own name, **angular frequency**, written ω (omega):

```formula
ω = 2 × π × f
ω = 2 × π × 440
ω ≈ 2764.6 rad/s
where
ω: omega, the angular frequency: how many radians the phase turns through per second, in radians per second (rad/s)
π: pi, about 3.14159
f: the ordinary frequency, in hertz (Hz), cycles per second
rad/s: radians per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: angular frequency is the frequency measured in radians per second instead of cycles per second, so it is 2π times bigger.
```

> [!note] Why the sine is special
> A sine contains exactly one frequency. Any periodic waveform (a sawtooth, a square, a recorded violin note) can be built by adding sines at whole-number multiples of its fundamental frequency. These are its **harmonics**, and the recipe of harmonic amplitudes is a big part of its **timbre**. The synthesis module builds on this.

## From time to samples

A digital synth doesn't compute x(t) for every possible t. It computes the wave at evenly spaced instants, `fs` times per second, where `fs` is the **sample rate** (48,000 per second is typical). Sample number n happens at time n/fs seconds, so the sine formula becomes:

```formula
x[n] = A × sin(2 × π × f × n / fs + φ)
where
x[n]: the value of sample number n (square brackets mean "the sample with this index", not a continuous time)
n: the sample index, a whole number counting up from 0
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second (equivalently hertz, Hz); typically 48,000
A: the amplitude, the largest value the wave reaches
sin: the sine function, taking an angle in radians
π: pi, about 3.14159
f: the frequency of the tone, in hertz (Hz)
φ: phi, the starting phase, in radians
In words: the sampled sine is the same formula with time replaced by "sample number divided by sample rate", which is the time at which that sample is taken.
```

Two derived numbers fall straight out of this, and the roadmap asks you to calculate both.

**Samples per period** tells you how many numbers describe one cycle:

```formula
S = fs / f
S = 48000 / 440
S ≈ 109.09
where
S: the number of samples in one cycle (samples per period); not usually a whole number
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second; here 48,000
f: the frequency of the tone, in hertz (Hz), cycles per second; here 440
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: divide samples per second by cycles per second to get samples per cycle. A 440 Hz cycle at 48 kHz spans about 109 samples.
```

**Phase increment** is how far round the cycle you move between one sample and the next. It's the reciprocal of samples per period:

```formula
Δp = f / fs
Δp = 440 / 48000
Δp ≈ 0.009167 cycles
Δθ = 2 × π × Δp ≈ 0.05760 rad
where
Δp: delta p, the phase increment in cycles per sample (the Greek letter Δ, delta, means "a step in")
Δθ: delta theta, the same increment measured in radians per sample
f: the frequency of the tone, in hertz (Hz)
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second
π: pi, about 3.14159
cycles: fractions of one full cycle
rad: radians; one full cycle is 2π radians
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: each sample moves the phase on by the frequency divided by the sample rate, in cycles; multiply by 2π to get radians.
```

The same calculation for several notes, in Python:

```python
import math

fs = 48_000
for f in (55, 440, 1000, 3520):
    spp = fs / f
    inc = f / fs
    rad = 2 * math.pi * inc
    print(f"{f:>4} Hz {spp:7.2f} spp"
          f" {inc:.6f} cyc {rad:.5f} rad")
```

```text
  55 Hz  872.73 spp 0.001146 cyc 0.00720 rad
 440 Hz  109.09 spp 0.009167 cyc 0.05760 rad
1000 Hz   48.00 spp 0.020833 cyc 0.13090 rad
3520 Hz   13.64 spp 0.073333 cyc 0.46077 rad
```

Notice:

- Samples per period is rarely a whole number. A 440 Hz cycle at 48 kHz takes 109.09 samples, so the samples land at slightly different points of each cycle. That's fine; the phase is tracked as a real number.
- Higher pitches get **fewer** samples per cycle. At 3520 Hz you have under 14 points per cycle. Lesson 4 shows where this runs out.
- The phase increment depends on **both** f and fs. Run the same code at 44.1 kHz and every increment changes. If a synth assumes the wrong sample rate, every note comes out at the wrong pitch.

## The phase accumulator

The formula above recomputes the phase from n each time. Real oscillators don't. They keep a running **phase** variable and add the increment each sample, wrapping it back into range after each full cycle:

```python
import math

fs, f = 48_000, 440.0
inc = f / fs
phase = 0.0          # cycles, in [0, 1)
out = []
for n in range(6):
    out.append(math.sin(2*math.pi*phase))
    phase += inc
    if phase >= 1.0:
        phase -= 1.0
print([round(x, 4) for x in out])
```

```text
[0.0, 0.0576, 0.1149, 0.1719, 0.2284, 0.284]
```

This **phase accumulator** is the core of many digital oscillators. It has three advantages over recomputing from n.

**1. Frequency changes are smooth.** If you recompute `sin(2π·f·t)` with a new f, the phase jumps. Switch from 440 Hz to 450 Hz at 0.525 s:

```python
import math
fs = 48_000
t = 25_200 / fs      # 0.525 s
before = math.sin(2*math.pi*440*t)
after  = math.sin(2*math.pi*450*t)
print(f"{before:.3f} -> {after:.3f}")
```

```text
0.000 -> 1.000
```

The output leaps from 0 to full scale in one sample: a click. With an accumulator, you just change `inc` and the phase carries on from where it was. Vibrato, pitch bends and glides all rely on this.

**2. Precision stays bounded.** The phase is always between 0 and 1, so its spacing stays bounded instead of getting coarser with elapsed time. Rounding of the increment and additions can still introduce a small frequency error. A sample counter n only grows. A 32-bit float (common on embedded chips) represents integers exactly only up to 2²⁴ = 16,777,216. At 48 kHz that's about 349.5 seconds, under six minutes. After that, `n + 1 == n` in float32, and an oscillator that computes from n starts to drift and distort.

**3. It's cheap.** One add and a compare per sample, then a waveform lookup. The waveform part can be `sin`, a table, or simple arithmetic for a sawtooth (the phase itself, rescaled, *is* a naive saw).

> [!warning] Keep the state between blocks
> Audio is processed in blocks (say 48 samples at a time). The phase must persist from one block to the next. If you reset it to zero each block, you get a click every block: at 48 samples per block and 48 kHz, that's a 1 kHz buzz.

## Pitfalls

- **Degrees passed to `sin`.** `math.sin(90)` is about 0.894, not 1. The argument is radians.
- **Forgetting the 2π.** `sin(f·t)` produces a tone 2π times too low (440 Hz becomes about 70 Hz).
- **Hard-coding the sample rate.** Compute the increment from the actual rate the audio hardware is running at.
- **Ignoring wrap.** Without the wrap, a float phase eventually loses precision like the counter does.

## Key takeaways
- Frequency is one divided by the period. Wavelength (speed of sound divided by frequency) is a distance in air and irrelevant inside the synth's maths.
- One cycle is 2π radians; `sin` takes radians.
- A sine is amplitude × sin(2π × frequency × time + starting phase); sampled, time becomes sample number divided by sample rate.
- Samples per period is the sample rate divided by the frequency; the phase increment is the frequency divided by the sample rate, in cycles per sample (2π times that in radians). Both depend on the sample rate.
- Oscillators keep a wrapped phase accumulator so that frequency changes preserve phase and numerical spacing stays bounded; abrupt changes can still create transients and rounding error remains. Keep that state across processing blocks.

## Further reading
- [Sinusoids — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA)](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Sinusoids.html)
- [Sine wave — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_wave)
- [Phase (waves) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_(waves))
- [Speed of sound — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_sound)
- [Numerically controlled oscillator (phase accumulator) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerically_controlled_oscillator)

questions.prompt: A bass note has a frequency of 250 Hz. What is its period?

options.explanation: Correct. The period is one divided by the frequency: 1/250 of a second is 0.004 s, which is 4 ms.
0.25 ms is 1/4000 s, the period of a 4 kHz tone: 16 times too short. The period of 250 Hz is 1/250 s.
This treats the frequency number as if it were milliseconds. A 250 ms period would be a 4 Hz wave, far below hearing.
Off by a factor of ten. 40 ms is the period of 25 Hz.

questions.workedExample:
Period and frequency are reciprocals: the period is how long one cycle takes, the frequency is how many cycles fit in a second.

```formula
T = 1 / f
T = 1 / 250 Hz
T = 0.004 s
T = 4 ms
where
T: the period, the time one cycle takes, in seconds (s)
f: the frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 250 Hz
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second; 0.004 s × 1000 = 4 ms
In words: the period is one divided by the frequency, so a 250 Hz note repeats every 4 milliseconds.
```

Sanity check: 250 cycles of 4 ms each fill 1000 ms, which is one second.

questions.prompt: Your synth runs at a sample rate of 48,000 Hz. How many samples does one cycle of a 200 Hz sine take?

options.explanation: This confuses the frequency with the number of samples per cycle. The answer depends on the sample rate too.
This multiplies the sample rate by the frequency. Samples per period is a ratio: the sample rate divided by the frequency.
This is the frequency divided by the sample rate, the phase increment in cycles per sample, which is the reciprocal of what was asked.
Correct. Samples per period is the sample rate divided by the frequency: 48,000 / 200 = 240.

questions.workedExample:
Samples per period answers "how many sample instants fit in one cycle?"

1. One cycle of 200 Hz lasts 1/200 s = 5 ms.
2. Samples arrive every 1/48,000 s ≈ 0.0208 ms.
3. 5 ms / 0.0208 ms = 240.

Or directly:

```formula
S = fs / f
S = 48000 / 200
S = 240
where
S: the number of samples in one cycle (samples per period)
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second; here 48,000
f: the frequency of the sine, in hertz (Hz), cycles per second; here 200
In words: samples per second divided by cycles per second gives samples per cycle.
```

The reciprocal, 200/48,000 ≈ 0.00417, is the phase increment in cycles per sample.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python print (rounded to 3 decimal places)?

```python
import math
print(round(math.sin(90), 3))
```

options.explanation: This assumes the argument is 90 degrees. Python's `math.sin` takes radians, so 90 means 90 radians, about 14.3 cycles.
Correct. 90 radians is not a quarter turn, and the sine of 90 radians is about 0.894. To get 1.0 you'd convert first with `math.radians(90)`, which gives π/2 radians.
sin is zero at whole multiples of π radians. 90 is not a multiple of π (90/π ≈ 28.65).

options.text: An error, because 90 is outside the range of sin
options.explanation: `sin` accepts any real number; it's periodic, so large inputs are fine.

questions.workedExample:
1. `math.sin` interprets its argument as radians, and one full cycle is 2π radians.
2. Work out how many cycles 90 radians is, and keep only the fractional part, because sine repeats every cycle:

```formula
p = 90 / (2 × π)
p ≈ 14.32 cycles
0.324 × 360° ≈ 116.6°
sin(90) ≈ 0.894
where
p: the angle of 90 radians expressed in cycles (whole turns)
π: pi, about 3.14159; 2π radians is one full cycle
cycles: whole turns of the wave; the 14 complete turns don't change the sine
sin: the sine function; Python's version takes radians
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 90 radians is 14 full turns plus about a third of a turn (0.324 of a turn, 116.6°), and the sine of that angle is about 0.894.
```

```python
import math
print(round(math.sin(90), 3))
# 0.894
print(math.sin(math.radians(90)))
# 1.0
```

In oscillator code this bug shows up when phase is kept in degrees or cycles and passed to `sin` without multiplying by π/180 or 2π.

questions.prompt: An oscillator runs at a sample rate of 44,100 Hz and must produce 1,000 Hz. What phase increment should it add each sample?

options.explanation: This is the sample rate divided by the frequency, which is samples per period. Adding 44.1 cycles each sample would jump the phase 44 full turns per sample.
1,000 is the number of cycles per *second*. Per sample, you divide by the number of samples per second.
Correct. The increment is the frequency divided by the sample rate: 1000 / 44,100 ≈ 0.022676 cycles, or about 0.14248 radians after multiplying by 2π.
The number is right but the unit isn't. 0.022676 is in cycles; in radians it's 2π times larger.

questions.workedExample:
The phase increment is cycles per second divided by samples per second, which gives cycles per sample.

```formula
Δp = f / fs
Δp = 1000 / 44100
Δp ≈ 0.022676 cycles
Δθ = 2 × π × Δp
Δθ ≈ 0.14248 rad
where
Δp: delta p, the phase increment in cycles per sample (Δ, delta, means "a step in")
Δθ: delta theta, the same increment in radians per sample
f: the wanted frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 1000
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second; here 44,100
π: pi, about 3.14159; one cycle is 2π radians
cycles: fractions of a full cycle
rad: radians
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: each sample, move the phase on by 1000/44,100 of a cycle, which is about 0.142 radians.
```

Check: after 44,100 samples (one second), 44,100 × 0.022676 ≈ 1000 cycles. ✓

Whichever unit your accumulator uses, wrap it at the matching full cycle (1.0 or 2π).

questions.prompt: An oscillator's code computes `inc = f / 48000` because the developer assumed 48 kHz. The board's codec is actually running at 44.1 kHz. A note requested at 440 Hz is played. What frequency comes out?

options.explanation: Correct. Each sample advances 440/48,000 of a cycle, and 44,100 samples happen per second: 44,100 × 440/48,000 = 404.25 Hz, almost a semitone and a half flat.

options.text: 440 Hz, because the frequency is set in the code
options.explanation: The code sets cycles *per sample*, not per second. How many samples happen per second is decided by the hardware clock.
This is 440 × 48,000/44,100, which would be the result if the code assumed 44.1 kHz and the hardware ran at 48 kHz. Here it's the other way round.
The rates differ by a ratio of 0.919, not 0.5, so the pitch drops by about 147 cents, not 1200.

questions.workedExample:
The code fixes how far the phase moves *per sample*. The hardware decides how many samples happen *per second*.

```formula
Δp = 440 / 48000 ≈ 0.009167
f_out = fs × Δp
f_out = 44100 × 440 / 48000
f_out = 404.25 Hz
where
Δp: delta p, the phase increment the code computed, in cycles per sample
fs: the sample rate the hardware actually runs at, in samples per second; here 44,100
f_out: the frequency that actually comes out, in hertz (Hz)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: cycles per sample times samples per second gives cycles per second, so the note comes out at 440 × 44,100/48,000 = 404.25 Hz.
```

How far flat is that, in musical terms? Cents (lesson 2) measure the size of a frequency ratio:

```formula
c = 1200 × log_2(f_out / f)
c = 1200 × log_2(404.25 / 440)
c ≈ −147 cents
where
c: the pitch difference in cents; 100 cents is one semitone
log_2: the base-2 logarithm, which answers "2 to what power gives this number?"
f_out: the frequency that comes out, 404.25 Hz
f: the frequency that was requested, 440 Hz
cents: hundredths of a semitone
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the output is about 147 cents, nearly a semitone and a half, flat.
```

Every note is flat by the same ratio. Always derive the increment from the sample rate the audio driver reports.

questions.prompt: Which statements about phase are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Adding two identical sines that are 180° (π radians) out of phase gives silence
options.explanation: Correct. At every instant one is the negative of the other, so the sum is zero.

options.text: A sudden jump in an oscillator's phase partway through a note is usually heard as a click
options.explanation: Correct. A phase jump makes the waveform value change abruptly between two samples, and that step contains energy at many frequencies.

options.text: A steady sine started a quarter-cycle late sounds clearly different from one started on time
options.explanation: A constant phase offset on a single steady tone is essentially inaudible. Phase matters when signals are combined or when it changes abruptly.
Hertz is cycles per second, a unit of frequency. Phase is a position in the cycle: radians, degrees or fractions of a cycle.

options.text: π/2 radians is the same phase as 90°
options.explanation: Correct. A full cycle is 2π radians or 360°, so a quarter of a cycle, π/2 radians, is 90°.

questions.workedExample:
Go through each statement:

1. **Cancellation:** shifting a sine by half a cycle flips its sign, so the two waves sum to zero at every instant. ✓

```formula
sin(θ + π) = −sin(θ)
where
sin: the sine function, taking an angle in radians
θ: theta, any phase angle, in radians
π: pi, about 3.14159; π radians is half a cycle (180°)
In words: half a cycle later, a sine has exactly the opposite value, so adding the two gives silence.
```

2. **Phase jump:** the next sample lands at a new point in the cycle, making a step in the waveform. Steps are broadband (they contain energy at many frequencies), so you hear a click. ✓
3. **Static offset:** your ear doesn't hear the absolute starting phase of a lone steady tone. ✗
4. **Units:** hertz measures frequency (cycles per second); phase is an angle. ✗
5. **Conversion:** 360° is 2π radians, so 90°, a quarter of that, is π/2 radians. ✓

questions.prompt: An oscillator resets phase to zero every 64-sample block at 48 kHz while attempting a 440 Hz sine. The same truncated waveform repeats each block. What is its repetition frequency?

options.explanation: 440 Hz is the intended oscillator setting. Resetting every block replaces it with a waveform repeating at the block rate.
64 is the block size in samples, not a frequency.
That's the Nyquist frequency for 48 kHz, which isn't related to how often the reset happens.
Correct. The identical 64-sample block repeats 48,000/64 = 750 times per second, producing a 750 Hz harmonic series rather than preserving a separate 440 Hz tone.

questions.workedExample:
The repeated block is a waveform in its own right, and its frequency is how often it repeats.

```formula
t_b = N_b / fs
t_b = 64 / 48000 s ≈ 1.333 ms
r = 1 / t_b
r = 48000 / 64 = 750 Hz
where
t_b: the duration of one block, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
N_b: the block size, in samples; here 64
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second; here 48,000
r: the repetition rate of the block, in hertz (Hz)
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
Hz: hertz, repetitions per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: one block lasts 64/48,000 of a second, so a waveform that restarts every block repeats 750 times a second.
```

A 440 Hz cycle is about 109.1 samples long, so 64 samples isn't a whole number of cycles. Each reset cuts the wave at a non-zero point, producing a click 750 times a second.

The fix is to store `phase` in the oscillator object so it carries over from one block to the next.

questions.prompt: In air at about 20 °C, roughly what is the wavelength of a 100 Hz tone, and how does it affect the samples your synth generates?

options.text: About 3.43 m, so the synth needs at least 3.43 m of buffer memory
options.explanation: Wavelength is a physical distance in air, not an amount of memory. One cycle is 480 samples at 48 kHz, whatever the wavelength.

options.text: About 3.43 m; it has no effect on the sample values, which depend only on frequency, amplitude, phase and sample rate
options.explanation: Correct. Wavelength is the speed of sound divided by the frequency: 343/100 ≈ 3.43 m. Wavelength describes the sound once it travels through air; the samples are a function of time.

options.text: About 0.29 m; it sets how many samples are in each cycle
options.explanation: 0.29 is 100/343, the reciprocal of the right ratio. And samples per cycle comes from the sample rate divided by the frequency, not the wavelength.

options.text: About 34,300 m; it's why low notes need more processing
options.explanation: This multiplies c by f instead of dividing. Low notes don't need more processing per sample.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
λ = c / f
λ = 343 / 100
λ ≈ 3.43 m
where
λ: lambda, the wavelength, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound, in metres per second (m/s); about 343 m/s in dry air at 20 °C
f: the frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 100
m: metres
m/s: metres per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: a 100 Hz sound wave in air is about 3.43 m from one pressure peak to the next.
```

In the synth, the waveform is a sequence of numbers over time:

```formula
x[n] = A × sin(2 × π × f × n / fs + φ)
where
x[n]: the value of sample number n
n: the sample index, counting 0, 1, 2, …
A: the amplitude
sin: the sine function, taking radians
π: pi, about 3.14159
f: the frequency, in hertz (Hz)
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second
φ: phi, the starting phase, in radians
In words: each sample depends on amplitude, frequency, phase and sample rate. There's no distance, so the wavelength never appears.
```

Wavelength matters later, for room acoustics and speaker placement.

questions.prompt:
An oscillator on a chip that only has fast 32-bit floats computes each sample directly from a sample counter `n`, which is a float32 incremented by 1 each sample:

```formula
x[n] = sin(2 × π × f × n / fs)
where
x[n]: the output sample number n
sin: the sine function, taking radians
π: pi, about 3.14159
f: the oscillator frequency, in hertz (Hz)
n: the sample counter, stored as a 32-bit float
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second; here 96,000
In words: the phase is recomputed from the ever-growing sample counter every sample.
```

At a sample rate of 96 kHz, after about how long does `n + 1` stop changing `n`?

options.explanation: This would correspond to 2²¹ at 96 kHz. float32 has a 24-bit significand (23 bits stored plus an implicit leading 1), so the limit is 2²⁴.

Correct. float32 represents every integer exactly up to 2²⁴ = 16,777,216. At 96,000 samples per second that's 16,777,216 / 96,000 ≈ 174.8 s ≈ 2.9 min. Beyond it, adding 1 rounds back to the same value.
This is 2³²/96,000, the limit of a 32-bit unsigned *integer* counter. A float32 has only 24 bits of precision.

options.text: Never, because floats have a huge range
options.explanation: The *range* of float32 goes up to about 3.4 × 10³⁸, but its *precision* is fixed at 24 significant bits. Large values have large gaps between neighbours.

questions.workedExample:
1. float32 = 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 23 stored fraction bits plus an implicit leading 1 → 24 bits of precision.
2. All integers up to 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 are exact. Above that, the spacing between floats is 2, so 2²⁴ + 1 rounds to 2²⁴.
3. Convert that sample count to time:

```formula
t = 2^24 / fs
t = 16777216 / 96000 s
t ≈ 174.8 s ≈ 2.9 min
where
t: the time until the counter stops increasing, in seconds (s)
fs: the sample rate, in samples per second; here 96,000
s: seconds
min: minutes
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the counter runs out of exact integers after 16,777,216 samples, which at 96,000 samples a second is just under 3 minutes.
```

In practice the phase loses precision well before that, because the calculation multiplies a large number (n) by a small one (f/fs). A wrapped phase accumulator in [0, 1) avoids the problem entirely.

questions.prompt: An oscillator is playing 440 Hz and must change to 880 Hz partway through a note. Which methods avoid a sudden jump in the *output value* (a click)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the phase accumulator and set the increment to the 880 Hz value at once
options.explanation: Correct for the output-value discontinuity asked about: phase is retained. The abrupt change in slope can still create a transient; smoothing pitch makes the transition gentler.

options.text: Keep the phase accumulator and ramp the increment from the 440 Hz value to the 880 Hz value over 50 ms
options.explanation: Correct. This is a glide (portamento). The phase stays continuous throughout.

options.text: From the change onwards, compute `sin(2π·880·t)` using the absolute time t
options.explanation: Wrong: a 880 Hz sine and a 440 Hz sine both computed from absolute time are at unrelated phases at the moment of the switch, so the output generally jumps.

options.text: Reset the phase to 0 and start the 880 Hz cycle from there
options.explanation: Wrong: the output jumps from wherever the 440 Hz wave was to the sine of zero, which is 0. Unless the old wave happened to be at an upward zero crossing, that's a step.

questions.workedExample:
The key idea is that **phase must be continuous** for the waveform to be continuous.

- Accumulator, instant increment change: phase at the change point is unchanged → output continuous. ✓
- Accumulator, ramped increment: same, plus a smooth pitch change. ✓
- Recomputing from absolute time: the phase jumps from one formula to the other. ✗
- Resetting the phase: a deliberate discontinuity. ✗

For the absolute-time method, compare the phase just before and just after the switch:

```formula
θ_before = 2 × π × 440 × t
θ_after = 2 × π × 880 × t
where
θ_before: the phase in radians used just before the switch
θ_after: the phase in radians used just after it
π: pi, about 3.14159
t: the absolute time since the note (or the program) started, in seconds
In words: at the switch the new phase is double the old one, so the two only point to the same place in the cycle by coincidence; usually the output steps.
```

This is why oscillators are designed around a phase accumulator.

questions.prompt:
A developer makes a glide by computing each output value directly from absolute time:

```formula
x = sin(2 × π × f(t) × t)
where
x: the output value
sin: the sine function, taking radians
π: pi, about 3.14159
f(t): the glide's frequency setting at time t, in hertz (Hz); it rises in a straight line from 440 Hz to 880 Hz between t = 10.0 s and t = 10.1 s
t: the absolute time, in seconds (s)
In words: the code multiplies the current frequency setting by the total elapsed time to get the phase.
```

What is the *instantaneous* frequency halfway through, at t = 10.05 s?

options.text: 660 Hz, the value of f(t) at that moment
options.explanation: This assumes the instantaneous frequency equals f(t). It's actually the rate of change of the phase, and the phase here is f(t) × t, whose rate of change has a second term.

options.text: 880 Hz, because the glide is heading there
options.explanation: The target is reached at 10.1 s. And even then, the formula gives a different answer.
4,400 Hz per second is the slope of f(t), how fast the setting rises. You need to multiply it by t (10.05 s) and add f(t).

Correct. The phase in cycles is f(t) × t. Its rate of change is f(t) plus t times the slope of f(t): 660 + 10.05 × 4,400 = 44,880 Hz. That's above the audio band, so the glide comes out as a burst of garbage.

questions.workedExample:
Instantaneous frequency is the rate of change (the derivative) of phase, measured in cycles, with respect to time. The phase here is a product of two things that both depend on time, so the product rule from calculus gives two terms.

```formula
φ(t) = f(t) × t
dφ/dt = f(t) + t × f′(t)
f′(t) = (880 − 440) / 0.1 = 4400 Hz/s
dφ/dt = 660 + 10.05 × 4400
dφ/dt = 44880 Hz
where
φ(t): phi, the phase in cycles at time t
f(t): the frequency setting at time t, in hertz (Hz); 660 Hz halfway through the glide
t: the absolute time, in seconds (s); here 10.05 s
dφ/dt: the rate of change of phase with respect to time (d means "a tiny change in"), which is the instantaneous frequency, in hertz (Hz)
f′(t): f prime, the slope of the frequency setting: how fast it rises, in hertz per second (Hz/s)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
Hz/s: hertz per second
In words: because the code multiplies the frequency setting by the total elapsed time, the frequency you hear is the setting plus elapsed time times how fast the setting is changing, which is enormous 10 seconds in.
```

The later in the piece the glide happens, the worse it gets, because t multiplies the slope. A phase accumulator integrates the frequency sample by sample (adding the frequency divided by the sample rate each sample), so its instantaneous frequency is always exactly f.

lessons.title: Pitch and tuning
lessons.summary: Octaves, semitones and equal temperament; converting MIDI note numbers to hertz; cents and detuning; why pitch is logarithmic; and the difference between pitch and timbre.
lessons.body:
A synth receives "play note 60" and has to turn it into a phase increment. Between those two is a formula you'll write in your first afternoon and use for the rest of the project. Understanding it properly also explains why pitch bends, detune and vibrato are specified in semitones and cents, not hertz.

## Pitch is a ratio, not a difference

**Frequency** is physical: cycles per second. **Pitch** is perceptual: how high or low a note sounds. For a steady periodic tone, the pitch we hear closely tracks the **fundamental frequency** (the rate at which the whole waveform repeats).

The crucial fact is that our ears judge pitch by **ratios**. Going from 110 Hz to 220 Hz sounds like the same step as going from 440 Hz to 880 Hz, even though the first is a 110 Hz difference and the second is 440 Hz. Both are a doubling, and a doubling of frequency is an **octave**.

```text
A1    A2    A3    A4    A5
55 -> 110 -> 220 -> 440 -> 880 Hz
  x2    x2    x2    x2
```

So pitch is **logarithmic** in frequency: equal steps in pitch are equal *multiplications* of frequency. This is the single most important idea in the lesson.

## Exponentials and logarithms, briefly

Two identities do almost all the work. The first says that adding in an exponent (the small raised number, "the power") multiplies the result:

```formula
2^(a + b) = 2^a × 2^b
2^(1 + 0.5) = 2 × 1.414 ≈ 2.83
where
2^a: 2 raised to the power a: a copies of 2 multiplied together (fractional and negative powers are allowed, e.g. 2^0.5 ≈ 1.414 and 2^−1 = 0.5)
a: any number, here an amount of octaves
b: any other number, here another amount of octaves
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: adding exponents multiplies the results. Transposing up an octave (+1 in the exponent) doubles the frequency, whatever note you started on.
```

The second undoes the first. The base-2 logarithm answers "how many doublings make x?":

```formula
2^y = x
y = log_2(x)
log_2(8) = 3
log_2(1.5) ≈ 0.585
log_2(x) = ln(x) / ln(2)
where
log_2: the base-2 logarithm, the inverse of "2 to the power of"
x: any positive number, typically a frequency ratio
y: the number of doublings (octaves) that make x
ln: the natural logarithm (base e ≈ 2.718), which every maths library has; dividing by ln(2) converts it to base 2
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: if 2 to the power y gives x, then y is the base-2 logarithm of x, so log_2 counts doublings. 8 is three doublings of 1, and a ratio of 1.5 is a little over half a doubling.
```

Most languages offer `log2`; otherwise use the last line, which works because any logarithm divided by the same logarithm of 2 gives the base-2 version. Logarithms are defined only for positive numbers, which is fine here: frequencies and their ratios are always positive.

The practical rule follows: **do pitch arithmetic in note space, then convert to hertz once at the end.** In note space, transposing, bending and modulating are simple additions. In hertz they're multiplications, and mixing the two up is a classic bug.

## Semitones and equal temperament

Western music divides the octave into 12 **semitones**. In **twelve-tone equal temperament** (12-TET), every semitone has the same frequency ratio. Twelve of them must make an octave (×2), so each one is the number that gives 2 when 12 copies of it are multiplied together:

```formula
r = 2^(1/12)
r ≈ 1.059463
r^12 = 2
where
r: the frequency ratio of one 12-TET semitone (no unit: it's a ratio)
2^(1/12): 2 to the power one-twelfth, the twelfth root of 2
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: each semitone up multiplies the frequency by about 1.0595, and twelve of those steps exactly double it.
```

For example, the note one semitone above A4 (440 Hz) is A♯4, at 440 × 1.059463 ≈ 466.16 Hz.

That irrational ratio is the price of a tuning where every key is equally in tune. Simple whole-number ratios such as 3:2 (the pure ratio of a perfect fifth) don't land exactly on a 12-TET note:

| Interval | Just ratio | 12-TET ratio | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Octave | 2.000 | 2.000 | 0 cents |
| Fifth | 1.500 | 1.4983 | 12-TET 1.96 cents flat |
| Major third | 1.250 | 1.2599 | 12-TET 13.69 cents sharp |

The difference column uses **cents**, defined below. Almost all synths default to 12-TET; alternative tunings are a later feature.

## MIDI note numbers

MIDI identifies notes with a number from **0 to 127**. Note **60 is middle C**, and **69 is the A above it**, which is tuned to **440 Hz** by convention. Each step of 1 is one semitone. Your synth needs to turn a note number into a frequency, and the standard conversion (the Wikipedia article on the MIDI Tuning Standard gives it) is:

```formula
f = 440 × 2^((n − 69) / 12)
f = 440 × 2^((60 − 69) / 12)
f = 440 × 2^(−0.75)
f ≈ 261.63 Hz
where
f: the frequency to play, in hertz (Hz)
n: the MIDI note number, 0 to 127 (or a fractional value once bends and detune are added); here 60, middle C
440: the reference frequency of note 69 (A4), in hertz
69: the note number of A4, the reference note
12: semitones per octave
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: count semitones away from A4 (n − 69), divide by 12 to get octaves, raise 2 to that power to get a frequency ratio, and multiply by 440 Hz.
```

Going the other way, a tuner or a pitch detector turns a frequency back into a (usually fractional) note number:

```formula
n = 69 + 12 × log_2(f / 440)
n = 69 + 12 × log_2(880 / 440)
n = 69 + 12 × 1 = 81
where
n: the note number, fractional in general; the nearest whole number is the nearest note
f: the measured frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 880 Hz
log_2: the base-2 logarithm, which counts doublings
440: the reference frequency of A4, in hertz
69: the note number of A4
12: semitones per octave
In words: count how many octaves the frequency is above or below 440 Hz, turn that into semitones (× 12), and add it to 69. 880 Hz is exactly one octave up, note 81.
```

Both formulas assume 12-TET and A4 = 440 Hz; another tuning system or reference pitch changes the constants.

```python
def midi_to_hz(n, a4=440.0):
    return a4 * 2 ** ((n - 69) / 12)

for n in (0, 21, 57, 60, 69, 81, 108, 127):
    print(f"{n:>3} {midi_to_hz(n):9.2f} Hz")
```

```text
  0      8.18 Hz
 21     27.50 Hz
 57    220.00 Hz
 60    261.63 Hz
 69    440.00 Hz
 81    880.00 Hz
108   4186.01 Hz
127  12543.85 Hz
```

Notes 21 to 108 are the 88 keys of a piano (A0 to C8). Note 0, at about 8.2 Hz, is below hearing; you'd hear it only through its harmonics.

> [!warning] Octave labels vary, numbers don't
> In scientific pitch notation middle C is **C4**, so note 60 = C4 and 69 = A4. Some software and instruments label note 60 as C3 instead: Ableton Live, for example, calls middle C "C3". The number on the wire is always 60, so think in note numbers and check how each piece of gear displays them.

Keep the 440 as a parameter (`a4` above). A "master tune" control is just a different reference.

## Cents

A **cent** is 1/100 of a 12-TET semitone, so there are 1200 cents per octave. To measure how far apart two frequencies are in pitch, count the octaves between them and multiply by 1200:

```formula
c = 1200 × log_2(f_2 / f_1)
c = 1200 × log_2(445 / 440)
c ≈ 19.6 cents
where
c: the interval from f_1 up to f_2, in cents (negative if f_2 is lower)
f_1: the reference frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 440 Hz
f_2: the other frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 445 Hz
log_2: the base-2 logarithm, which counts octaves in a frequency ratio
cents: hundredths of a semitone; 1200 make an octave
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 445 Hz is about 19.6 cents (a fifth of a semitone) above 440 Hz.
```

To shift a frequency by a number of cents, undo the logarithm:

```formula
f_2 = f_1 × 2^(c / 1200)
where
f_2: the shifted frequency, in hertz (Hz)
f_1: the starting frequency, in hertz (Hz)
c: the shift in cents (positive is sharp, negative is flat)
In words: a shift of c cents multiplies the frequency by 2 to the power c/1200, the same ratio on every note.
```

How small is a cent? Below what most people can hear as a pitch change. Published figures for the just-noticeable difference vary: one commonly cited summary gives about 3 Hz for sine tones below 500 Hz (roughly 12 cents at 440 Hz, and far more at bass frequencies) and about 0.6%, roughly 10 cents, above 1 kHz. Some sources quote 5–6 cents for attentive listeners. It varies with frequency, level, timbre, context and the listener, so treat any single number as a rough guide. Two tones played together are another matter: even a cent or two of mistuning can be heard as slow beating.

Cents are the natural unit for **detune**. Here's a function that finds the nearest note and how far off it is:

```python
import math

NAMES = ["C", "C#", "D", "D#", "E", "F",
         "F#", "G", "G#", "A", "A#", "B"]

def hz_to_note(f, a4=440.0):
    m = 69 + 12 * math.log2(f / a4)
    n = round(m)
    cents = 100 * (m - n)
    name = NAMES[n % 12] + str(n // 12 - 1)
    return n, name, cents

for f in (261.63, 450.0, 430.0, 100.0):
    n, name, c = hz_to_note(f)
    tag = f"{c:+.1f}c"
    print(f"{f:.2f} ->", n, name, tag)
```

```text
261.63 -> 60 C4 +0.0c
450.00 -> 69 A4 +38.9c
430.00 -> 69 A4 -39.8c
100.00 -> 43 G2 +35.0c
```

The `n // 12 − 1` gives the octave number in scientific pitch notation, because note 0 is C−1.

## Detuning and beats

Play two oscillators at nearly the same frequency and you hear the level wobble. That's **beating**: the two sines drift in and out of phase, reinforcing then cancelling. The wobble happens once for every cycle one oscillator gains on the other, so its rate is the difference in frequency. Detune one 440 Hz oscillator by +10 cents:

```formula
f_2 = 440 × 2^(10 / 1200) ≈ 442.55 Hz
f_beat = |f_1 − f_2|
f_beat = |440 − 442.55| ≈ 2.55 Hz
where
f_1: the first oscillator's frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 440 Hz
f_2: the detuned oscillator's frequency, in hertz (Hz)
f_beat: the beat rate, how many times per second the level swells and dips, in hertz (Hz)
|…|: absolute value: the size of the difference, ignoring its sign
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the level wobbles at the difference between the two frequencies, here about 2.55 times a second.
```

This holds for two tones close in frequency (within a few hertz to a few tens of hertz); tones far apart don't produce an audible wobble.

Because the detune is in cents, the *beat rate* grows with pitch: the same 10 cents at 880 Hz beats at about 5.1 Hz. This is why a fixed-cents detune sounds "wider" in the high register, and some synths offer a fixed-Hz detune as an alternative.

## Linear vs exponential modulation

Suppose an LFO adds vibrato. Two ways to do it:

1. **Linear (in Hz):** add a fixed number of hertz.
2. **Exponential (in pitch):** multiply by a fixed ratio, set in cents.

```formula
f_lin = f_0 + D × L
f_exp = f_0 × 2^(d × L / 1200)
where
f_lin: the frequency with linear (hertz) vibrato, in hertz (Hz)
f_exp: the frequency with exponential (pitch) vibrato, in hertz (Hz)
f_0: the note's unmodulated frequency, in hertz (Hz)
L: the LFO's current output, swinging between −1 and +1
D: the linear vibrato depth, in hertz (Hz); for example 10 Hz
d: the exponential vibrato depth, in cents; for example 39 cents
In words: linear vibrato swings the frequency by the same number of hertz on every note; exponential vibrato swings it by the same musical interval on every note.
```

With D of 10 Hz, a 440 Hz note swings about ±39 cents. At 110 Hz the same ±10 Hz swings about +151 and −165 cents, a much wider wobble. With exponential vibrato, d sets the depth in cents, and it sounds equally deep on every note.

Option 2 is what players expect for vibrato and pitch bend. MIDI pitch bend, for example, is normally interpreted as a number of semitones (the bend range), added in note space.

Analogue synths face the same problem in hardware. The common **1 volt per octave** standard, popularised by Moog, makes control voltage linear in pitch: each extra volt doubles the oscillator frequency, using an exponential converter inside the oscillator.

```formula
f = f_0 × 2^V
f = 110 × 2^2 = 440 Hz
where
f: the oscillator frequency, in hertz (Hz)
f_0: the frequency the oscillator plays at 0 V, in hertz (Hz); here 110 Hz
V: the control voltage, in volts (V); here 2 V. Strictly it's V divided by 1 volt, so the exponent has no unit
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: every extra volt of control voltage raises the pitch one octave, and 1/12 V raises it one semitone.
```

Real oscillators only follow this law over a limited range, which is why analogue synths need calibrating.

## Pitch vs timbre

Play a sine and a sawtooth at 220 Hz. They have the **same pitch** but sound completely different. The difference is **timbre**, often loosely called "tone colour".

A sawtooth at 220 Hz contains sine components at 220, 440, 660, 880 Hz and so on: the **harmonic series**, every whole-number multiple of the fundamental. In an ideal sawtooth their amplitudes fall off steadily:

```formula
f_k = k × f_0
a_k = 1 / k
where
f_k: the frequency of harmonic number k, in hertz (Hz)
k: the harmonic number, a whole number 1, 2, 3, …; k = 1 is the fundamental
f_0: the fundamental frequency, in hertz (Hz); here 220 Hz
a_k: the amplitude of harmonic k, relative to the fundamental (no unit)
In words: harmonic k sits at k times the fundamental and, in a sawtooth, has 1/k of its amplitude: the 3rd harmonic of 220 Hz is at 660 Hz with a third of the amplitude.
```

A sine has only the 220 Hz component. Because all the extra components are exact multiples, the waveform still repeats every 1/220 s, and the ear still hears 220 Hz.

The harmonic series is also where just ratios come from: harmonics 2, 3, 4, 5 give an octave, a fifth above that, another octave, and a major third. The 5th harmonic of 110 Hz is 550 Hz, about 14 cents below the 12-TET C♯5 (554.37 Hz).

Timbre also depends on how the sound changes over time: the attack, how harmonics fade, noise. Subtractive synthesis works by starting with a harmonically rich wave and filtering harmonics away, changing timbre while leaving pitch alone. That's the next module.

> [!note] The missing fundamental
> Pitch perception isn't just "find the lowest component". If you remove the 220 Hz component from a sawtooth and keep 440, 660, 880 Hz and so on, most listeners still hear a pitch of 220 Hz, because the harmonics are spaced 220 Hz apart. This is why small speakers can suggest bass notes they can't reproduce.

## Pitfalls

- **Adding hertz for musical intervals.** "Up a fifth" is ×1.4983, not +220 Hz.
- **Integer division.** In C-family languages, `(n − 69) / 12` with integers truncates to whole octaves. Use floating point.
- **Assuming octave labels.** Use note numbers between systems.
- **Converting too early.** Keep pitch as a float note number (including bend, detune and modulation in semitones), then convert to hertz, then to a phase increment.

## Key takeaways
- Pitch is perceived logarithmically: an octave is ×2 in frequency, a 12-TET semitone about ×1.0595 (the twelfth root of 2).
- Note number to frequency: 440 Hz times 2 to the power (note − 69)/12. Note 60 is middle C, 69 is A 440 Hz.
- An interval in cents is 1200 times the base-2 logarithm of the frequency ratio; 100 cents per semitone. Detune in cents; two close tones beat at the difference of their frequencies.
- Do pitch maths in note space, then convert once to hertz and then to a phase increment.
- Same pitch, different harmonic content = different timbre.
